# Water surfaces (R4)

Research only, 2026-10-01. No site code changed. Feeds task 78: a pool or
puddle surface over a photograph, like our glass panes. It ripples under the
cursor and under rain. Every light on the list lights it (the cursor lamp, the
room). It refracts the photograph below, reflects the room and the lights, and
throws caustics onto the photograph. It runs in our one raw WebGL1 context
([`gl.ts`](../../src/effects/engine/gl.ts)).

Every claim has a source link. **(computed)** marks a number worked out here
from a cited formula, and says how. **(estimate)** marks a judgement that no
source states. Code links to evanw/webgl-water are pinned to its last commit,
`73eda8b` (2016-01-07), which I cloned on 2026-10-01.

This builds on [tools-survey.md §6](tools-survey.md) (the decision to port
webgl-water), on [water-drops.md §3.1, §3.4 and §5](water-drops.md) (the lens
formula, area-ratio caustics, and the first list of water prior art), and on
the existing glass optics in `src/effects/optics`.

Pages I could not read:

- Springer, "Experiments on ring wave packet generated by water drop"
  ([s11434-008-0246-0](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1007/s11434-008-0246-0)):
  HTTP 429, rate-limited.
- Donelan & Plant 2009, "A threshold for wind-wave growth"
  ([10.1029/2008JC005238](https://agupubs.onlinelibrary.wiley.com/doi/abs/10.1029/2008JC005238)):
  HTTP 403. Only its search snippet was seen (it mentions a 0.18 m/s
  threshold, quantity not shown), so it is not used for a number.
- The PNAS/PMC water-strider raindrop paper
  ([PMC10835078](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC10835078/)): blocked
  by a captcha.
- Hugo Elias's original page (web.archive.org is blocked here). I used the
  [ixm-ibrahim explainer](https://www.ixm-ibrahim.com/explanations/simulating-water-ripples)
  instead.
- The Wikimedia Commons image files. The category pages loaded, but the image
  bytes did not, so the photos in §6 were **chosen by title and description,
  not viewed**.

## 0. Short answer

- **Approach: port** Evan Wallace's heightfield simulation and its two caustic
  ideas (MIT). Rewrite the shading in our own optics: our Fresnel, our room
  reflection, our light list. Wallace's shading is tuned by eye: it reflects
  **25%** straight down, where water reflects **2.04%**. Don't port it.
- **The simulation** is the 2D wave equation on a grid. Wallace's update
  ([water.js L49–78](https://github.com/evanw/webgl-water/blob/73eda8be832b649367b25ea5690c1f0181bb56ad/water.js#L49-L78))
  is `v += 2·(avg4 − h); v *= 0.995; h += v`. That is
  `c²Δt²/Δx² = 0.5`, exactly at the 2D stability limit **(computed, §1.2)**.
  It runs two steps per frame whatever the frame rate. We keep the equation,
  and add:
  - real units (mm, s);
  - a fixed sub-step;
  - wave speed set from physics, **c ≈ 0.23 m/s**, the slowest a ripple can
    travel ([Wikipedia: Capillary wave](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Capillary_wave));
  - damping that kills short ripples faster, as viscosity does
    (`e^(−2νk²t)`,
    [JFM 2024](https://www.cambridge.org/core/journals/journal-of-fluid-mechanics/article/experimental-investigation-of-surfactant-effects-on-gravitycapillary-wave-dissipation-and-surface-flow/34CA9B8C58953FD5F64EDBF75BDEE2C3)).
- **Optics, top-down:**
  - **Reflectance** is 2.04% straight on and still under 3% up to 45°
    **(computed, Fresnel at n = 1.333)**. The room reflection is faint. What
    shows is the **glints of each lamp**.
  - **No total internal reflection** happens looking down from air. Snell's
    window (about 97°) exists only for an eye under the water.
  - **Absorption is invisible at puddle depths.** 5 mm of pure water passes
    99.9% of red **(computed from
    [Pope & Fry 1997](https://omlc.org/spectra/water/data/pope97.txt))**.
    A pool's blue-green needs metres of water.
- **Refraction and caustics use the formula the glass already uses.** A slope
  ∇h shifts the point seen on the photograph by `(1 − 1/n)·d·∇h`. Caustic
  brightness is `1 / det(I + (1 − 1/n)·d·Hess h)`, which is the same as
  `causticAt` in
  [floor-light-shader.ts L176–188](../../src/lib/floor-light-shader.ts) with
  the water's Hessian put in.
  - For a puddle or a tray (d below about 10 cm), the caustic net stays short
    of its focus **(computed, §4.3)**. That one per-pixel formula is then
    correct, and it needs no extension.
  - Only a deep "pool" setting needs Wallace's scatter mesh. That uses
    `OES_standard_derivatives`, at 99.99%
    ([web3dsurvey](https://web3dsurvey.com/webgl/extensions/OES_standard_derivatives)).
- **Raindrops make rings.** A raindrop makes a crater, a stalk (jet), then
  rings of capillary-gravity waves
  ([Bliven, NASA, 2003](https://apps.dtic.mil/sti/pdfs/ADA499775.pdf)).
  - The rings have a characteristic wavelength of **about 3 cm**.
  - For 2.2–2.8 mm drops they are **0.05–0.1 mm high** at 13 cm and 800 ms.
  - They carry **1–2%** of the drop's kinetic energy
    ([Craeye et al. 1999](https://pure.tue.nl/ws/files/1414355/Metis133016.pdf)).
- **Wind.** The first wavelets appear at about **1.8 m/s** of wind, at
  **2.5 cm** and **9 Hz**
  ([Cavaleri et al. 2024](https://journals.ametsoc.org/view/journals/phoc/54/3/JPO-D-23-0217.1.xml)).
  Our dispersion relation gives 9.6 Hz at 2.5 cm **(computed)**, which agrees.

## 1. Reading webgl-water

Repo: [evanw/webgl-water](https://github.com/evanw/webgl-water). Every source
file carries "Copyright 2011 Evan Wallace, Released under the MIT license"
(e.g.
[water.js L1–7](https://github.com/evanw/webgl-water/blob/73eda8be832b649367b25ea5690c1f0181bb56ad/water.js#L1-L7)).
There is no LICENSE file. It uses Wallace's own `lightgl.js` helper, also MIT
([lightgl.js L1–7](https://github.com/evanw/webgl-water/blob/73eda8be832b649367b25ea5690c1f0181bb56ad/lightgl.js#L1-L7)).

### 1.1 Files

| File | Lines | What it is | Port? |
|---|---|---|---|
| `water.js` | 172 | The simulation: drop, update, normal and sphere-displacement shaders; ping-pong textures | **Port** (the core) |
| `renderer.js` | 353 | Shading: ray-traced pool box, sphere, caustic mesh pass, water surface shader | **Port two ideas** (the caustic mesh, the refracted-ray projection). Rewrite the rest |
| `main.js` | 281 | Input, timing (two sim steps per frame), sphere physics | **Ideas only** (drag adds drops) |
| `OES_texture_float_linear-polyfill.js` | 130 | Tests whether float textures filter linearly, by rendering a 2×2 texture and reading back | **Idea** (the same probe for half-float) |
| `cubemap.js`, `lightgl.js`, `*.jpg` | – | Sky cubemap, GL helper, tile texture | **No.** We have `environment.ts` and `gl.ts` |

### 1.2 The heightfield simulation (which equation)

**State.** An RGBA float texture, 256×256, holding
`(height, velocity, normal.x, normal.z)`
([water.js L9, L23–24](https://github.com/evanw/webgl-water/blob/73eda8be832b649367b25ea5690c1f0181bb56ad/water.js#L9-L24)).
Two textures ping-pong: each pass reads A, draws B and swaps them
([L152–161](https://github.com/evanw/webgl-water/blob/73eda8be832b649367b25ea5690c1f0181bb56ad/water.js#L152-L161)).

**Update**
([L49–78](https://github.com/evanw/webgl-water/blob/73eda8be832b649367b25ea5690c1f0181bb56ad/water.js#L49-L78)):

```
average = (h[x−1] + h[y−1] + h[x+1] + h[y+1]) / 4
v += (average − h) * 2.0
v *= 0.995
h += v
```

This is Müller's height-field wave equation
([GDC 2008 slides](https://media.gdcvault.com/gdc08/slides/S6509i1.pdf)):
`f = c²·(u[i+1,j] + u[i−1,j] + u[i,j+1] + u[i,j−1] − 4u[i,j])/h²`,
`v += f·Δt`, `u += v·Δt`. Wallace bakes in the constants.

- **(computed)** `2·(average − h) = 0.5·(Σ4 − 4h)`, so `c²Δt²/Δx² = 0.5`.
- **(computed, von Neumann)** For this semi-implicit (symplectic) Euler step
  on the 5-point Laplacian, the largest eigenvalue of the discrete Laplacian
  is `8/Δx²`. The step is stable when `ω_max·Δt ≤ 2`, i.e.
  `c²Δt²/Δx² ≤ 0.5`. **Wallace sits exactly on the limit.** The 0.995 factor
  is what keeps it bounded.
  - Müller states the 1D-style bound "c < h/Δt"
    ([slides](https://media.gdcvault.com/gdc08/slides/S6509i1.pdf)). The 2D
    five-point bound is tighter by √2.
- **Damping.** `0.995` per step is Müller's "scaling (unphysical, more direct
  control): v = s·v" (same slides). It damps every wavelength equally.
  - **(computed)** At 120 steps/s (60 fps × 2), `0.995¹²⁰ = 0.548` per
    second, an amplitude half-life of 1.15 s.
- **Frame-rate dependence.** `update()` calls `stepSimulation()` twice per
  animation frame, and ignores `seconds` for the water
  ([main.js L227–257](https://github.com/evanw/webgl-water/blob/73eda8be832b649367b25ea5690c1f0181bb56ad/main.js#L227-L257)).
  On a 120 Hz screen the waves run twice as fast. **Fix this when porting.**
- **Wave speed in the demo (computed).** The pool is 2 units wide, so
  Δx = 2/256. `c = √0.5·Δx/Δt = 0.66` units/s: a ripple crosses the pool in
  about 3 s.
- **Boundaries.** Texture clamping makes the edges reflect. Müller: "Clamp
  yields wave reflection", "Wrap yields periodic propagation"
  ([slides](https://media.gdcvault.com/gdc08/slides/S6509i1.pdf)).

The **three.js `webgl_gpgpu_water`** example (MIT) uses the same scheme in
Hugo Elias's form:
`newHeight = ((N + S + E + W)·0.5 − previous)·viscosity`, with viscosity 0.93
per frame on a 128² grid
([webgl_gpgpu_water.html L157, L198, L774](https://github.com/mrdoob/three.js/blob/dev/examples/webgl_gpgpu_water.html)).
Two buffers (current and previous) replace height and velocity, with the same
`C² = 0.5` **(computed)**.

**Sources of waves.**

- **Drop**
  ([water.js L30–48, L126–137](https://github.com/evanw/webgl-water/blob/73eda8be832b649367b25ea5690c1f0181bb56ad/water.js#L30-L48)):
  - `h += strength · (0.5 − 0.5·cos(π·max(0, 1 − r/radius)))`, a raised-cosine
    bump.
  - The demo starts with 20 drops of radius 0.03 and strength ±0.01
    ([main.js L85–87](https://github.com/evanw/webgl-water/blob/73eda8be832b649367b25ea5690c1f0181bb56ad/main.js#L85-L87)).
  - Dragging adds one drop per mouse event
    ([main.js L141–151](https://github.com/evanw/webgl-water/blob/73eda8be832b649367b25ea5690c1f0181bb56ad/main.js#L141-L151)).
- **Moving sphere**
  ([water.js L95–123, L139–150](https://github.com/evanw/webgl-water/blob/73eda8be832b649367b25ea5690c1f0181bb56ad/water.js#L95-L123)):
  - It adds the volume the sphere occupied last frame and subtracts what it
    occupies now, with a soft profile `exp(−(1.5t)⁶)`.
  - So it **conserves water volume**, and the wake comes out of the
    simulation by itself.
  - This is the model to port for a finger or cursor dipped in the water.

### 1.3 Normals

- **The normal pass**
  ([water.js L79–94](https://github.com/evanw/webgl-water/blob/73eda8be832b649367b25ea5690c1f0181bb56ad/water.js#L79-L94))
  uses **forward differences**: `cross(dy, dx)`, normalised, storing only
  `.xz`. The consumer rebuilds `y = √(1 − x² − z²)`
  ([renderer.js L162](https://github.com/evanw/webgl-water/blob/73eda8be832b649367b25ea5690c1f0181bb56ad/renderer.js#L162)).
- **Renou merges** the update and normal passes into one shader
  ([threejs-caustics `update_fragment.glsl`](https://github.com/martinRenou/threejs-caustics/blob/master/shaders/simulation/update_fragment.glsl)).
  BSD-3; I read the clone at its last commit, 2020-08-27.
- **The "peaked" hack.** Before shading, the surface shader walks 5 times
  along the normal (`coord += info.ba·0.005`) to make the water look "more
  peaked"
  ([renderer.js L156–160](https://github.com/evanw/webgl-water/blob/73eda8be832b649367b25ea5690c1f0181bb56ad/renderer.js#L156-L160)).
  It is a look, not physics.

**For us:** drop the normal pass. The consumers (glass compose, floor light)
take **central differences** for ∇h and a 9-tap stencil for the Hessian, in mm.
That is the same data `waveSlope`/`waveHessian` give for the glass's waviness
([waviness.ts L60–86](../../src/effects/optics/waviness.ts)). The texture then
only needs two channels (h, v). Do not port the peaked hack, or only as a lab
toggle.

### 1.4 Caustics (the area ratio)

Wallace's method
([medium write-up](https://medium.com/@evanwallace/rendering-realtime-caustics-in-webgl-2a99a29a0b2c)):
"Each vertex of the mesh represents a ray of light". "An increase in the area
of the triangle means the light has been spread out and must be dimmed. An
area decrease means the light has been focused and should be brighter."

In code
([renderer.js L228–302](https://github.com/evanw/webgl-water/blob/73eda8be832b649367b25ea5690c1f0181bb56ad/renderer.js#L228-L302)):

1. **Draw the water grid as a mesh** (`GL.Mesh.plane({detail: 200})`, so
   80 000 triangles,
   [L113](https://github.com/evanw/webgl-water/blob/73eda8be832b649367b25ea5690c1f0181bb56ad/renderer.js#L113))
   **into a 1024² caustic texture**
   ([L112](https://github.com/evanw/webgl-water/blob/73eda8be832b649367b25ea5690c1f0181bb56ad/renderer.js#L112)).
2. **In the vertex shader**, compute two landing points on the pool floor:
   - `oldPos`: the flat surface, refracted by the flat normal;
   - `newPos`: the displaced surface, refracted by the real normal
     (`refract(−light, normal, 1/1.333)`).
   - Position the vertex at `newPos`
     ([L241–253](https://github.com/evanw/webgl-water/blob/73eda8be832b649367b25ea5690c1f0181bb56ad/renderer.js#L241-L253)).
3. **In the fragment shader**, with `OES_standard_derivatives`:
   - `oldArea = |dFdx(oldPos)|·|dFdy(oldPos)|`, and the same for `newPos`;
   - output `oldArea/newArea · 0.2`
     ([L261–268](https://github.com/evanw/webgl-water/blob/73eda8be832b649367b25ea5690c1f0181bb56ad/renderer.js#L261-L268)).
   - **The 0.2 leaves headroom up to 5× in an 8-bit target.**
   - Without derivatives it writes a flat 0.2.
4. **Overlapping triangles add.** Where the light folds (past a focus),
   several sheets land on the same texel and add up. That is correct for
   strong caustics.
5. **Receivers sample the texture.** The walls and the sphere sample it along
   the refracted light direction, times `caustic.r · 4` or `· 2`
   ([L53–62, L86–93](https://github.com/evanw/webgl-water/blob/73eda8be832b649367b25ea5690c1f0181bb56ad/renderer.js#L53-L93)).
6. **The same pass also writes:**
   - a soft blob shadow of the sphere (channel g,
     [L272–280](https://github.com/evanw/webgl-water/blob/73eda8be832b649367b25ea5690c1f0181bb56ad/renderer.js#L272-L280));
   - the pool rim's shadow
     ([L282–284](https://github.com/evanw/webgl-water/blob/73eda8be832b649367b25ea5690c1f0181bb56ad/renderer.js#L282-L284)).

Wallace notes the limit: it "only works in certain cases but it's perfect for
caustics due to the refraction of light through a planar body of water"
([write-up](https://medium.com/@evanwallace/rendering-realtime-caustics-in-webgl-2a99a29a0b2c)).

Renou's version
([`water_vertex.glsl`/`water_fragment.glsl`](https://github.com/martinRenou/threejs-caustics/tree/master/shaders/caustics))
does the same ratio. Instead of a box intersection, it marches the refracted
ray through an environment depth map (up to 50 steps), and it guards
`newArea == 0`.

**Our engine already has the gather form of this.**
`causticAt` returns `1/max(|det(I + s·Hess)|, soft)`, clamped to [0.2, 7], where
`soft` comes from the lamp's penumbra
([floor-light-shader.ts L176–188](../../src/lib/floor-light-shader.ts)).
It runs per pixel and needs no mesh. It is valid while the light has not yet
crossed a focus; §4.3 shows when that holds.

### 1.5 Refraction and reflection shading

The surface shader
([renderer.js L152–184](https://github.com/evanw/webgl-water/blob/73eda8be832b649367b25ea5690c1f0181bb56ad/renderer.js#L152-L184))
works like this:

- It reflects and refracts the eye ray with GLSL `reflect`/`refract`
  (IOR 1.333). Each ray is traced analytically against the pool box and the
  sphere (`intersectCube`, `intersectSphere`,
  [L22–43](https://github.com/evanw/webgl-water/blob/73eda8be832b649367b25ea5690c1f0181bb56ad/renderer.js#L22-L43)).
  Above the rim it reads the sky cubemap, plus a sun glint `pow(dot(light,
  ray), 5000)`
  ([L130–150](https://github.com/evanw/webgl-water/blob/73eda8be832b649367b25ea5690c1f0181bb56ad/renderer.js#L130-L150)).
- **Its Fresnel is not physical:**
  - above water, `mix(0.25, 1.0, (1 − cos θ)³)`, i.e. **25% reflection
    straight down**
    ([L178](https://github.com/evanw/webgl-water/blob/73eda8be832b649367b25ea5690c1f0181bb56ad/renderer.js#L178));
  - below water, `mix(0.5, 1.0, …)`
    ([L169](https://github.com/evanw/webgl-water/blob/73eda8be832b649367b25ea5690c1f0181bb56ad/renderer.js#L169)).
  - Real water reflects 2.04% at normal incidence (§4.1).
- **The tints `abovewaterColor (0.25, 1.0, 1.25)` and
  `underwaterColor (0.4, 0.9, 1.0)`**
  ([L12–13](https://github.com/evanw/webgl-water/blob/73eda8be832b649367b25ea5690c1f0181bb56ad/renderer.js#L12-L13))
  are a stylistic pool colour. They are not absorption (§4.4).

**For us:** the photograph is a plane at depth d under the surface. The ray
trace reduces to one ray–plane intersection. Reflection comes from our room
([environment.ts](../../src/effects/optics/environment.ts)) and our lamp
glints ([reflection.ts](../../src/effects/optics/reflection.ts)). Fresnel comes
from `fresnelSP(cos, 1, 1.333)`
([stack.ts L39](../../src/effects/optics/stack.ts)).

### 1.6 What to port, line by line

| Wallace | Our version | Why |
|---|---|---|
| Update shader, [water.js L49–78](https://github.com/evanw/webgl-water/blob/73eda8be832b649367b25ea5690c1f0181bb56ad/water.js#L49-L78) | **Port**, with uniforms `C² = (cΔt/Δx)²` (≤ 0.45), viscous damping `ν_eff·∇²v` and a uniform `γ`; fixed Δt sub-steps from the scheduler's dt | Real units; frame-rate independent; keeps a stability margin |
| Drop shader, [L30–48](https://github.com/evanw/webgl-water/blob/73eda8be832b649367b25ea5690c1f0181bb56ad/water.js#L30-L48) | **Port**, and add a "ring" profile option for raindrops (§3.3). Several drops per draw (a uniform array, or point sprites with additive blend) | One pass per drop is wasteful when rain makes ~10/s |
| Sphere displacement, [L95–123, L139–150](https://github.com/evanw/webgl-water/blob/73eda8be832b649367b25ea5690c1f0181bb56ad/water.js#L95-L150) | **Port** as "finger": the cursor pressed into the water | Volume-conserving; the wake emerges |
| Normal pass, [L79–94](https://github.com/evanw/webgl-water/blob/73eda8be832b649367b25ea5690c1f0181bb56ad/water.js#L79-L94) | **Drop it**; consumers use central differences | One pass fewer; mm units; a Hessian is needed anyway |
| Float/half-float choice, [L19–29](https://github.com/evanw/webgl-water/blob/73eda8be832b649367b25ea5690c1f0181bb56ad/water.js#L19-L29); `canDrawTo` check, [main.js L76–78](https://github.com/evanw/webgl-water/blob/73eda8be832b649367b25ea5690c1f0181bb56ad/main.js#L76-L78) | **Port the probe**, and add a CPU fallback instead of throwing (§2) | 7–10% of Android lacks half-float (§2) |
| Linear-filter polyfill probe | **Port the idea** for `OES_texture_half_float_linear`; otherwise sample NEAREST and interpolate by hand | Android 89% |
| Caustic mesh pass, [renderer.js L228–302](https://github.com/evanw/webgl-water/blob/73eda8be832b649367b25ea5690c1f0181bb56ad/renderer.js#L228-L302) | **Port** for the deep "pool" setting only. Project onto the photo plane, not a box. Drop the sphere and rim shadows. Additive blend; 0.2 scale when the target is RGBA8 | Correct past the focus (§4.3) |
| Surface shader, [L152–184](https://github.com/evanw/webgl-water/blob/73eda8be832b649367b25ea5690c1f0181bb56ad/renderer.js#L152-L184) | **Rewrite** in our glass compose: `refract` to the photo plane, our Fresnel, room, glints | Its Fresnel and tints are not physical |
| Sky cubemap, tiles, AO, sphere, box ray tracer | **Do not port** | Not our scene |

We keep the MIT notice in the header of the ported files, as with raindrop-fx
([water-drops.md §7.2](water-drops.md)).

## 2. What our engine needs (extensions, fallbacks)

**Today.** One WebGL1 context, no depth or stencil, and no float targets yet.
`beginPass` resets blend, scissor, viewport and textures
([gl.ts L93–118](../../src/effects/engine/gl.ts)). It does **not** unbind
framebuffers. The sim's ping-pong FBOs must call `bindFramebuffer(null)` when
they finish. Better, `beginPass` should do it, as already planned for drops in
[water-drops.md §7.5](water-drops.md) step 2.

| Need | Extension | Support | Fallback |
|---|---|---|---|
| Sim state in float, readable | `OES_texture_half_float` | 98.78%; Android 90.1% ([web3dsurvey](https://web3dsurvey.com/webgl/extensions/OES_texture_half_float)) | `OES_texture_float`, 99.28% ([tools-survey §0](tools-survey.md)) |
| Render into it | `EXT_color_buffer_half_float` | 99.29%; Android 93.01% ([tools-survey §0](tools-survey.md)) | `WEBGL_color_buffer_float`, 98.59%; Android 91.69% ([web3dsurvey](https://web3dsurvey.com/webgl/extensions/WEBGL_color_buffer_float)). Then the **CPU sim** (below). Always probe with `checkFramebufferStatus`, as Wallace's `canDrawTo` does |
| Bilinear reads of the state | `OES_texture_half_float_linear` | 98.66%; **Android 89.08%** ([web3dsurvey](https://web3dsurvey.com/webgl/extensions/OES_texture_half_float_linear)) | NEAREST plus manual bilinear in the consumer (4 taps), or Wallace's NEAREST fallback ([water.js L22, L26](https://github.com/evanw/webgl-water/blob/73eda8be832b649367b25ea5690c1f0181bb56ad/water.js#L22-L26)) |
| Caustic scatter mesh (pool mode only) | `OES_standard_derivatives` | 99.99%; iOS, Android, Windows and macOS 100% ([web3dsurvey](https://web3dsurvey.com/webgl/extensions/OES_standard_derivatives)) | The per-pixel gather (`causticAt`), which needs no extension |
| Caustic accumulation above 1 | a half-float target, additive blend | as above | RGBA8 with Wallace's ×0.2 scale ([renderer.js L265](https://github.com/evanw/webgl-water/blob/73eda8be832b649367b25ea5690c1f0181bb56ad/renderer.js#L265)) |
| Drawing many raindrops in one call | `ANGLE_instanced_arrays` (core in WebGL1 practice) | (already used by the drop plan, [water-drops.md §6.2](water-drops.md)) | One dynamic quad buffer |

**The CPU fallback (our design, estimate).** When no float target is
renderable:

- Run the same update in TypeScript on a `Float32Array`, at **128²** cells.
- Upload it with `texSubImage2D`:
  - as `FLOAT` if `OES_texture_float` exists (uploading needs no render
    support);
  - otherwise as RGBA8 with height packed into two bytes.

The iWave paper reports a software 128×128 surface "at over 30 fps on GHz
processors", and that is with a 13×13 kernel
([Tessendorf](https://jtessen.people.clemson.edu/reports/papers_files/Interactive_Water_Surfaces.pdf)).
Our 5-tap update is about 30× cheaper per cell **(computed: 169/5 taps)**.
**About 0.3–0.6 ms a frame for 4 sub-steps (estimate, measure with
`?perf=1`).** The same TypeScript is the JS twin for the vitest checks (§7.4),
so the fallback costs no extra code.

**Context loss.** The sim textures die with the context. On restore, start
flat: water at rest is a valid state. Listen through `onSharedGlLoss`
([gl.ts](../../src/effects/engine/gl.ts)).

**Idle.** A still puddle is still. When `max|v|` and `max|h|` drop below
ε (0.001 mm, estimate) and nothing is driving the water, return `false` from
the scheduler step and stop ([scheduler.ts L64, L87](../../src/effects/engine/scheduler.ts);
the pattern is in [water-drops.md §7.5](water-drops.md)).

## 3. Physics: speed, damping, rain, wind

Constants: σ = 0.074 N/m and ρ = 1000 kg/m³ for water–air
([Wikipedia: Dispersion (water waves)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dispersion_(water_waves))),
g = 9.81 m/s², ν = 1.0×10⁻⁶ m²/s.

### 3.1 Ripple speed: capillary–gravity dispersion

`ω² = (g·k + σk³/ρ)·tanh(k·h)`
([Wikipedia: Dispersion (water waves)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dispersion_(water_waves))).

- Below 0.4 cm, waves are capillary; above 7 cm, they are gravity waves
  (same source).
- The **minimum phase speed is 0.23 m/s, at λ = 1.7 cm**
  ([Wikipedia: Capillary wave](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Capillary_wave)).

**(computed)** From that relation (deep water):

| λ | f | phase speed c | group speed c_g |
|---|---|---|---|
| 3 mm | 133 Hz | 40 cm/s | 59 cm/s |
| 5 mm | 64 Hz | 32 cm/s | 45 cm/s |
| 1 cm | 25 Hz | 25 cm/s | 31 cm/s |
| 1.7 cm | 13.7 Hz | **23.2 cm/s (min)** | 23.4 cm/s |
| 2.5 cm | 9.6 Hz | 24 cm/s | 20 cm/s |
| 4.4 cm | 6.4 Hz | 28 cm/s | **17.8 cm/s (min)** |
| 10 cm | 4.0 Hz | 40 cm/s | 21 cm/s |

**(computed) Shallow water.** In a puddle the depth hardly matters at these
wavelengths:

- at 5 mm depth: 1 cm ripples 24.9 cm/s, 5 cm ripples 22.1 cm/s;
- at 2 mm depth: 5 cm ripples slow to 14.7 cm/s
  (`tanh(kh)`, √(gh) = 14 cm/s).

**What this means for the simulation:**

- Every ripple a person sees on a puddle travels at **18–32 cm/s**. One wave
  speed, **c = 23 cm/s**, is within about ±30% of all of them **(computed)**.
- On screen, 1 CSS px is 1/96 in, i.e. **0.2646 mm**
  ([CSS Values: absolute lengths](https://www.w3.org/TR/css-values-4/#absolute-lengths)).
  So c ≈ **880 CSS px/s** at true scale **(computed)**: a ring crosses a
  1000 px puddle in about 1.1 s.
- **The real effect a single c misses is dispersion.** In a drop's ring
  packet, short capillary ripples run ahead at 30–60 cm/s, and the longer
  waves trail. Craeye et al. see it: "High-frequency wave precedes main rings"
  ([1999](https://pure.tue.nl/ws/files/1414355/Metis133016.pdf)).
- A 5-point wave equation is non-dispersive, except for grid error, which
  goes the wrong way (short waves *slower*). §5 lists the fix if it shows:
  iWave.
- **Wakes.** An object moving slower than the minimum phase speed cannot
  feed any wave that keeps pace with it, so it makes no wake.
  **(computed)** Stationary waves need `c(k) = U`, and that has no solution
  for `U < 23 cm/s`, i.e. **below about 880 px/s**. A slow finger makes a
  moving dimple; a fast one makes a V wake.

### 3.2 Damping

- **Viscosity.** On a clean surface the amplitude decays as `e^(−2νk²t)`
  ([JFM 2024, eq. in §2](https://www.cambridge.org/core/journals/journal-of-fluid-mechanics/article/experimental-investigation-of-surfactant-effects-on-gravitycapillary-wave-dissipation-and-surface-flow/34CA9B8C58953FD5F64EDBF75BDEE2C3)).
  **(computed)** e-folding times: 0.11 s at 3 mm; 0.32 s at 5 mm; 1.3 s at
  1 cm; 3.7 s at 1.7 cm; 7.9 s at 2.5 cm; 32 s at 5 cm. **Short ripples die
  fast, and long ones linger.** This is why a disturbed puddle smooths into
  long slow undulations.
- **Real water damps more.** The same JFM study measured spatial decay rates
  of 0.84, 2.25 and 4.80 m⁻¹ at 12, 24 and 36 Hz in clean water. With a
  surfactant (Triton X-100) they were 1.11, 3.15 and 6.20 m⁻¹. "The measured
  decay rates are significantly higher than the theoretical".
  - So a "cleanliness" factor of **×1 to ×1.4** is measured. Up to ×3 for a
    dirty puddle is an **(estimate)**.
- **(computed) Wallace's uniform 0.995** equals the viscous decay of
  λ ≈ 1.15 cm waves for every wavelength. It looks right for the middle band.
  It is too weak for short ripples, which then stay as grid noise, and too
  strong for long swells.
- **In the update.** Use viscous diffusion of velocity:
  `v += 4ν_eff·∇²v·Δt`.
  - **(computed)** For a mode, `ẍ + 4νk²ẋ + ω²x = 0` gives an amplitude decay
    of `e^(−2νk²t)`.
  - Explicit diffusion is stable while `4ν_eff·Δt/Δx² ≤ 0.25`. At Δx = 1.5 mm
    and Δt = 4 ms that is about 0.007 for clean water **(computed)**, far
    inside the limit.
  - Add a small uniform `γ` for bottom friction in very shallow puddles
    **(estimate)**.
- **Edges.**
  - **Wall** (a tray, a pool): reflect (clamp).
  - **Beach** (a real puddle's sloping rim): absorb, using a damping band a
    few cells wide. Chentanez & Müller use perfectly matched layers with
    "λ_decay = 0.9 and λ_update = 0.1"
    ([hfFluid.pdf](https://matthias-research.github.io/pages/publications/hfFluid.pdf)).

### 3.3 How raindrops make rings

- **The sequence.** A raindrop hitting water makes a cavity with a crown. It
  collapses "into a vertical stalk of water, which subsides to spawn rings of
  gravity-capillary waves that propagate outward"
  ([Bliven, Oceans 2003](https://apps.dtic.mil/sti/pdfs/ADA499775.pdf)). The
  spectra are narrow and log-Gaussian.
- **Measured rings** ([Craeye, Sobieski, Bliven & Guissard 1999, IEEE JOE](https://pure.tue.nl/ws/files/1414355/Metis133016.pdf)):
  - drops of 2.2 and 2.8 mm, from 1, 3 and 5.5 m;
  - a characteristic wavenumber of about 0.2 mm⁻¹, i.e. **λ ≈ 3 cm**.
    Le Méhauté's theory gives 43 mm;
  - **height at 13 cm and 800 ms: about 0.1 mm** (2.8 mm drops) and
    **0.05 mm** (2.2 mm);
  - the disturbed ring is about **6 cm wide**;
  - **1–2% of the kinetic energy** goes into rings for 2.8 mm drops, under 1%
    for 2.2 mm;
  - **high frequencies lead.**
- **Fall speeds.**
  - Atlas et al. (1973): `v(D) = 9.65 − 10.3·e^(−0.6D)` m/s, with D in mm
    ([quoted in Ulbrich 1994](https://arrc.ou.edu/~chilson/Papers/ulbrich+94_jtech.pdf);
    [Klaassen 1988](https://research.rug.nl/files/14670260/1988JAtmosSciKlaassen.pdf)).
  - Drizzle falls at about 2 m/s, and a 5 mm drop at about 9 m/s
    ([Physics Factbook](https://hypertextbook.com/facts/2007/EvanKaplan.shtml)).
  - **(computed)** v(2.8 mm) = 7.7 m/s, and its kinetic energy is 343 µJ.
- **Sizes.** Marshall–Palmer: `N(D) = N₀·e^(−ΛD)`, with N₀ = 8000 m⁻³mm⁻¹ and
  `Λ = 4.1·R^−0.21` mm⁻¹ (R in mm/h)
  ([Wikipedia: Raindrop size distribution](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Raindrop_size_distribution)).
- **(computed) Impacts per second**, ∫N(D)·v(D)dD over 0.1–6 mm:

  | Rain | Λ | median-volume D₀ = 3.67/Λ | Impacts per m²·s | On a 26×18 cm puddle (1000×700 px) | Of those, ≥ 1 mm |
  |---|---|---|---|---|---|
  | 1 mm/h | 4.1 | 0.9 mm | 1 540 | 72/s | ~2/s |
  | 5 mm/h | 2.9 | 1.3 mm | 3 270 | 153/s | **~11/s** |
  | 20 mm/h | 2.2 | 1.7 mm | 6 000 | 281/s | ~40/s |

  - The "≥ 1 mm" share is `e^(−Λ·0.9)` of the drops above 0.1 mm
    **(computed)**.
  - Marshall–Palmer is known to overcount the smallest drops. Spawn only
    D ≥ 0.5 mm, and let the rest be a fine "fizz" noise **(estimate)**.
- **What to stamp.** A raindrop is an impulse that sets off a packet. In a
  non-dispersive simulation a single raised-cosine bump leaves one crest and
  one trough. To see the several concentric crests in the photographs (§6),
  stamp a radially **oscillating** profile into the velocity:
  - two or three cycles of λ ≈ 3 cm (Craeye), under a Gaussian envelope of
    about 6 cm (Craeye's ring width), with zero net volume;
  - amplitude scaled so the ring reads **0.05–0.1 mm at 13 cm**, and by D³·v²
    (kinetic energy) across drop sizes **(estimate, calibrate against the
    Craeye numbers in a test)**.
  - The stalk is a sub-mm-wide vertical jet. Seen from above, it would show at
    most as a brief glint **(estimate)**. Skip it.

### 3.4 Wind

- The minimum wind for the first wavelets in the open sea is **close to
  1.8 m/s**. The wavelets are **2.5 cm long at 9 Hz**, and at 2.2 m/s they are
  4–15 mm high. They "quickly disappear as soon as the developing wind waves
  take a leading role"
  ([Cavaleri, Langodan, Pezzutto & Benetazzo 2024, JPO](https://journals.ametsoc.org/view/journals/phoc/54/3/JPO-D-23-0217.1.xml)).
  The paper says this is lower than previously assumed. It found the
  "Phillips" mechanism (random pressure forcing) active in the field.
- **(computed)** 2.5 cm at 9.6 Hz is on the dispersion curve in §3.1, so the
  simulation's single c (23 cm/s, versus 24 cm/s for 2.5 cm) is right for
  wind ripples.
- **Model** **(estimate)**:
  - Below 1.8 m/s: nothing.
  - Above it: add Phillips-style forcing to v. That is a low-amplitude noise
    pressure field drifting downwind at about the wind speed, in patches,
    because gusts make "cat's-paws".
  - Raise its strength with (U − 1.8).
- **Indoors there is no wind.** A puddle in a photography site's "room" should
  default to 0.

## 4. Optics

### 4.1 Fresnel at n = 1.333

**(computed)** With the full equations (as `fresnelSP` in
[stack.ts L39](../../src/effects/optics/stack.ts)), unpolarised, air to
water:

| Angle of incidence | 0° | 20° | 30° | 45° | 60° | 70° | 80° | 85° |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| Reflectance | **2.04%** | 2.06% | 2.14% | 2.79% | 5.97% | 13.4% | 34.8% | 58.4% |

- F₀ = ((n−1)/(n+1))² = 0.0204, half of float glass's 4.2%
  ([reflection.ts](../../src/effects/optics/reflection.ts)).
- **Brewster's angle is 53.1°** (atan 1.333) **(computed)**. Reflections near
  there are strongly s-polarised. That matters only if the polariser filter
  ever applies to water.
- **For our camera** (looking straight at the page,
  [environment.ts](../../src/effects/optics/environment.ts)): ripple slopes
  of 0.03–0.13 (§4.3) tilt the normal by only 2–7°. So **the room reflection
  is 2.0–2.1% everywhere: faint.** What reads as "water" is:
  - the **lamp glints**. A smooth surface (roughness ≈ 0) gives a sharp image
    of the lamp disc, broken by the ripples into moving highlights. Use the
    existing GGX glint with n = 1.333 and the lamp radius;
  - the **refraction wobble** of the photograph;
  - the **caustic net**.

### 4.2 Snell's window and total internal reflection

- **Critical angle: asin(1/1.333) = 48.6°** **(computed)**.
- Underwater, "an underwater viewer sees everything above the surface through
  a cone of light of width of about 96 degrees". It "compresses a 180° angle
  of view above water to a 97°". Outside the cone is dark or a total-internal-
  reflection image, and "ripples or waves … cause local distortions or
  complete disintegration of the image"
  ([Wikipedia: Snell's window](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Snell%27s_window)).
- **For our top-down view: no TIR.** A ray from air always enters the water,
  refracted to at most 48.6° **(computed)**. Snell's window only matters for
  an "under the water looking up" view. Nothing in task 78 asks for that. If
  one is ever added (looking up at the room through the surface), the window
  and the TIR fix from [water-drops.md §3.2](water-drops.md) apply.

### 4.3 Refraction of the photograph, and caustic brightness

**(computed) Paraxial derivation** (the same as the drop lens in
[water-drops.md §3.1](water-drops.md), but the light ends **inside** the
water):

- A surface tilted by slope p bends a vertical ray by
  `θ_i − θ_t ≈ p·(1 − 1/n) = 0.25·p`, toward the crest.
  - For comparison, a thin film on glass, which the ray leaves into air,
    bends it by `(n−1)·p` ([water-drops.md §3.1](water-drops.md)).
- **View.** The point of the photograph seen through surface point x is
  `x + (1 − 1/n)·d·∇h` (d = water depth). Under a crest the photograph is
  magnified, like a convex lens.
- **Apparent depth.** The photograph also appears raised to `d/n`. Feed
  `d/n` into the viewpoint parallax as the gap
  ([viewpoint.ts `behindGlassShift`](../../src/effects/optics/viewpoint.ts)).
- **Caustic.** Light from far above lands at `x + s·∇h`, with
  `s = (1 − 1/n)·d`. So the brightness on the photograph is
  `1/|det(I + s·Hess h)|`. That is exactly the `causticAt` formula, with
  `s = 0.25·d` for water.
  - A lamp at height H above the surface: scale s by `H/(H − d)`, the same
    magnification as the shadow model
    ([shadow.ts](../../src/effects/optics/shadow.ts)).
  - Blur by the lamp penumbra `R·d/(H − d)` (same file).
- **(computed) When does the gather formula hold?** A sinusoid of amplitude A
  and wavenumber k has a peak curvature of A·k², so it focuses at
  **`z_f = n/((n−1)·A·k²)`**:

  | Ripple | A | Peak slope | Focus depth z_f |
  |---|---|---|---|
  | 1 cm | 0.1 mm | 0.063 | 10 cm |
  | 1 cm | 0.05 mm | 0.031 | 20 cm |
  | 2.5 cm wind wavelet | 0.5 mm | 0.13 | 13 cm |
  | 3 cm rain ring | 0.1 mm | 0.021 | 91 cm |
  | 5 mm | 0.02 mm | 0.025 | 13 cm |

  - **A puddle or tray (d = 3–30 mm) is well short of focus.** The caustic is
    a gentle net, peak ratio about `1/(1 − d/z_f)`: about 1.1× for 1 cm of
    water under a 1 cm ripple of 0.1 mm. Per-pixel `causticAt` is exact
    there.
  - **Sharp, knotted pool-floor lines need d near z_f, i.e. 10 cm or more of
    water.** For the "pool" preset (d ≥ 5 cm, estimate), use Wallace's scatter
    mesh, which handles folding.
- **How bright real caustics get.**
  - Under the sea, at 0.5–3 m and 3–5 m/s wind, "maximum light flashes can
    exceed 7 E_d". With steeper waves, peaks "can exceed 11 E_d". The
    strongest measured flash was "in excess of 15 E_d", at 0.86 m
    ([Hieronymi & Macke 2012, Ocean Science](https://os.copernicus.org/articles/8/455/2012/os-8-455-2012.pdf)).
  - The most intense flicker is in light to moderate winds, 2–7 m/s (same
    source).
  - **Our existing clamp [0.2, 7]**
    ([floor-light-shader.ts L187](../../src/lib/floor-light-shader.ts)) matches
    the 7× figure. Allow up to about 12× in pool mode, still limited by the
    lamp penumbra floor **(estimate from Hieronymi & Macke)**.
- **Light conservation.** The mean of the ratio over a full ripple period is
  1 (the area ratio redistributes light, it does not create it). This is the
  test in §7.4.

### 4.4 Absorption tint by depth

Pure water, from [Pope & Fry 1997](https://omlc.org/spectra/water/data/pope97.txt)
(file in cm⁻¹, converted to m⁻¹): 0.0101 at 465 nm, 0.0565 at 550 nm, 0.264
at 610 nm, 0.34 at 650 nm. Our screen primaries are 610/550/465 nm
([scatter.ts](../../src/effects/optics/scatter.ts)).

**(computed)** Transmission `e^(−a·path)` (R, G, B):

| Path | R | G | B |
|---|---|---|---|
| 5 mm (puddle) | 0.999 | 1.000 | 1.000 |
| 3 cm (tray) | 0.992 | 0.998 | 1.000 |
| 30 cm | 0.92 | 0.98 | 1.00 |
| 1 m | 0.77 | 0.95 | 0.99 |
| 4 m (a 2 m pool, down and back) | 0.35 | 0.80 | 0.96 |

- **At page scale, pure water has no colour.** Wallace's cyan tints
  (§1.5) are a pool look, which needs metres of water. Tint does not belong
  on a puddle.
- Keep the absorption term as a cause, `σ_rgb`, with the pure-water values as
  default. A user can then pick "pool depth" or a dyed, tannin-brown or
  murky liquid. That is the same `exp(−σ·thickness)` term as blood in
  [water-drops.md §4](water-drops.md).
- The path is `2d` for light that goes down to the print and back up.

### 4.5 Lit by every light

Lights are a list ([lights.ts L45, L163](../../src/effects/light/lights.ts)).
For each light, the water layer contributes:

- **a caustic on the photograph**: the area ratio above, using that light's
  position, height and radius (point lamp, torch, flare);
- **a glint**: the GGX specular of that light off the water normal, at
  F(1.333);
- **the room**: the environment light, as a 2% Fresnel reflection of the HDR
  room ([environment.ts](../../src/effects/optics/environment.ts)).

The photograph itself is lit as it is today. The water only redistributes the
light (caustic) and attenuates it (Fresnel loss on entry, about 2%, and
`σ_rgb`).

## 6. Reference photographs

All on Wikimedia Commons, so the licence is on each file page. **Chosen by
title and category; the images themselves could not be downloaded here**
(§ top), so check each one before using it.

**Rain on puddles, rings.** Check ring count and spacing, short ripples
leading, and how fast the rings fade.

## 7. Decisions

### 7.1 Approach

1. **Port** Wallace's simulation core (MIT notice kept) into
   `src/effects/water/surface-sim.ts` (TS twin and CPU fallback) and
   `surface-sim.glsl.ts` (GPU). Changes:
   - real units (mm, s) through `1 CSS px = 0.2646 mm`
     ([CSS](https://www.w3.org/TR/css-values-4/#absolute-lengths)), with a
     lab scale override;
   - fixed sub-steps with `C = cΔt/Δx ≤ 0.67` (C² ≤ 0.45, a 10% margin under
     the 0.5 limit, §1.2) and an accumulator, so the result is frame-rate
     independent;
   - k-selective viscous damping (§3.2) instead of the uniform 0.995;
   - a "wall" or "beach" edge;
   - no normal pass; state in two channels (h, v).
2. **One height source.** The water heightfield is one more **height source**
   for the optics stack. It is read by the same consumer code as the glass
   waviness and the drop map ([water-drops.md §6](water-drops.md); the
   optics-engine "surface layer" step):
   - slope → the view offset `(1 − 1/n)·d·∇h`;
   - Hessian → the caustic `causticAt`;
   - normal → Fresnel and glints.
   Generalise `causticAt` to take a Hessian from any source instead of only
   `waveSurface`.
3. **Caustics.**
   - **Gather** (per pixel, no extension) for puddle and tray depths.
   - **Scatter** (Wallace's mesh, `OES_standard_derivatives`) only for the
     "pool" preset (d ≥ 5 cm, estimate), where §4.3 shows the light folds.
4. **Shading is ours:**
   - `fresnelSP(·, 1, 1.333)`;
   - the room through `environment.ts`;
   - GGX glints for every light on the list;
   - `exp(−σ_rgb·2d)` with Pope & Fry σ;
   - the apparent-depth parallax `d/n`.
   Do not port Wallace's 25% Fresnel or his tints.
5. **Fallbacks.** GPU half-float → GPU float → CPU 128² sim with texture
   upload → `minimal` tier: a still surface (glints only, no motion).
   `prefers-reduced-motion`: no rain, finger ripples damped ×5 **(estimate)**.
6. **Not now:** iWave dispersion (held, see §7.5), FFT ocean, full shallow-
   water flow.

### 7.2 Numbers

| Quantity | Value | Source |
|---|---|---|
| Wave speed c | **0.23 m/s ≈ 880 CSS px/s** at true scale | min phase speed ([Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Capillary_wave)); px **(computed)** |
| Grid spacing Δx | **1.5 mm (≈ 5.7 CSS px)**; a 1000×700 px puddle is 176×124 cells | **(estimate)**: resolves 6 mm ripples at 4Δx; rain rings are ~3 cm |
| Sub-step Δt | ≤ 0.67·Δx/c = **4.3 ms**, so 4 sub-steps per 60 Hz frame | **(computed)** from the §1.2 stability limit |
| Viscous damping | `4ν_eff·∇²v`, ν = 1.0×10⁻⁶ m²/s; cleanliness ×1 (clean) to ×3 (dirty) | `e^(−2νk²t)` ([JFM 2024](https://www.cambridge.org/core/journals/journal-of-fluid-mechanics/article/experimental-investigation-of-surfactant-effects-on-gravitycapillary-wave-dissipation-and-surface-flow/34CA9B8C58953FD5F64EDBF75BDEE2C3)); measured ×1.3–1.4 with surfactant; ×3 **(estimate)** |
| Index n | 1.333; F₀ = 2.04%; critical angle 48.6°; Brewster 53.1° | **(computed)** |
| View offset | `(1 − 1/n)·d·∇h = 0.25·d·∇h` | **(computed, §4.3)** |
| Caustic | `1/max(abs(det(I + 0.25·d·H/(H−d)·Hess h)), penumbra floor)`, clamp [0.2, 7] (puddle), up to 12 (pool) | **(computed, paraxial)**; `causticAt`; [Hieronymi & Macke](https://os.copernicus.org/articles/8/455/2012/os-8-455-2012.pdf) |
| Absorption σ (R, G, B) | 0.264, 0.0565, 0.0101 m⁻¹ (pure water) | [Pope & Fry](https://omlc.org/spectra/water/data/pope97.txt) |
| Default depth d | **8 mm** (a darkroom tray / puddle) | **(estimate)** |
| Rain ring | λ ≈ 3 cm, envelope ~6 cm, 0.05–0.1 mm at 13 cm/800 ms for 2.2–2.8 mm drops | [Craeye 1999](https://pure.tue.nl/ws/files/1414355/Metis133016.pdf) |
| Rain rate → impacts | Marshall–Palmer × Atlas fall speed; e.g. 5 mm/h → ~11 drops ≥ 1 mm per second on 26×18 cm | **(computed, §3.3)** |
| Wind threshold | 1.8 m/s; first wavelets 2.5 cm, 9 Hz | [Cavaleri 2024](https://journals.ametsoc.org/view/journals/phoc/54/3/JPO-D-23-0217.1.xml) |
| Finger wake threshold | 0.23 m/s ≈ 880 px/s | **(computed)** |

### 7.3 Lab controls (causes only)

Following the site rule "you set causes, physics sets effects"
([reflection.ts header](../../src/effects/optics/reflection.ts)):

- **Depth** (mm, 1–200). It drives refraction strength, caustic sharpness,
  tint, and the switch to scatter-mesh caustics.
- **Edge**: wall (tray, pool) or beach (puddle).
- **Cleanliness** (surfactant/dirt damping, ×1–×3).
- **Liquid tint** σ_rgb: pure water (default), pool-blue (metres of water),
  tannin, murky (with scatter).
- **Rain** (mm/h, 0–50).
- **Wind** (m/s, 0–5).
- **Finger**: press-and-drag dips the cursor into the water (Wallace's sphere
  displacement); the lamp stays the lamp.
- **Scale** (mm per CSS px, default 0.2646). Hidden: for a photo that
  represents a bigger scene.
- **Debug views** (not causes): height, |∇h|, the caustic ratio, the
  refracted lookup offset, sim cells, sub-steps per frame.

### 7.4 Tests

Each is a JS twin in vitest unless marked e2e, as for the glass
(`e2e/optics.spec.ts` checks the GLSL twins in real WebGL).

1. **Speed.** On a periodic grid, a plane wave of λ ≥ 8Δx travels at c
   within 3%.
2. **Stability.** Random initial state at C² = 0.45 for 10 000 steps: bounded,
   no NaN.
3. **Energy.** `Σ(½v² + ½c²|∇h|²)` is conserved to 1e-3 over 1 000 steps with
   damping off, and never increases with it on.
4. **Frame-rate independence.** One impulse stepped at 30, 60 and 144 Hz frame
   times: ring radius at t = 0.5 s equal within one cell, and equal to
   c·t ± 2 cells.
5. **k-selective damping.** Measured decay rates for λ = 6 mm and 3 cm match
   `2ν_eff·k²` within 5%.
6. **Volume.** Σh is unchanged by the finger (sphere displacement) and by ring
   stamps (zero net volume), to 1e-6.
7. **Optics.**
   - F(0°) = 0.0204; F(60°) = 0.0597.
   - No TIR for any ray from air.
   - View offset = 0.25·d·∇h.
   - Apparent depth = d/n.
8. **Caustic.**
   - The mean of the gather ratio over one ripple period is 1 within 2% for
     d < 0.5·z_f.
   - The scatter mesh and the gather agree within 5% at d = 0.3·z_f.
   - The scatter mesh shows folds (ratio > 7) at d ≈ z_f.
9. **Rain.** At 5 mm/h on a 26×18 cm puddle, the seeded spawner gives
   11 ± 3 drops ≥ 1 mm per second. The ring height at 13 cm and 800 ms for a
   2.8 mm drop is 0.1 mm ± 50% (calibrated against Craeye).
10. **e2e.**
    - `?try=water` keeps exactly two WebGL contexts (the `e2e/gl.spec.ts`
      pattern).
    - The framebuffer is unbound after the sim pass.
    - No frames run while the water is still (`e2e/scheduler.spec.ts`).
    - A stamped impulse's ring, read back, grows at c.
    - `?water=cpu` (forced fallback) matches the GPU ring within one cell.
    - `?perf=1` records `gpu:water-sim`, `gpu:water` and `cpu:water-sim`
      (the `e2e/perf.spec.ts` pattern).
11. **Side by side** with the §6 photographs: rings (Tuntorp, Kanagawa),
    caustic net (Myrstigen, Mallnitz), finger dimple (water striders). Then
    Ony approves.

Budgets to measure: sim ≤ 0.3 ms GPU desktop and ≤ 0.8 ms mobile; gather
caustic plus refraction ≤ 0.4 ms; CPU fallback ≤ 0.6 ms. All **(estimate)**,
in line with the drop budgets in [water-drops.md §6.4](water-drops.md).

### 7.5 Still unknown

- **Whether non-dispersive rings look right.** Real rings lead with short
  ripples (Craeye). If the side-by-side fails, build iWave with a
  capillary-gravity kernel (169 taps/cell). Its mobile cost is unmeasured.
- **The full ring-packet profile over time** (amplitude against radius and
  t). The 2008 Springer ring-packet paper could not be read (HTTP 429). The
  oscillating stamp in §3.3 is an estimate to calibrate.
- **Half-float precision.** Ripples are 0.01–0.1 mm on top of a resting level.
  Store h as the deviation from rest (it is) and check for drift over minutes.
- **Layer order with glass.** Is the water over the glass, under it, or
  replacing the pane? This decides whether the drop map and the water sim
  share a pass. It is a design question for Ony, not research.
- **Bottom friction in mm-deep puddles.** The extra damping is not quantified
  here (uniform γ, estimate).
- **The reference photos are unviewed** (downloads blocked). Confirm they show
  what their titles say.
